ops.why: Displaced by P-19: weakest Pattern in my judgment; its rule (evidence cannot grant task ownership) is already carried by the goal-check role text that names a change with no owning task as a plan/scope defect.

ops.entry: WHEN declaring a defect class closed DO run one probe one boundary beyond the stated class contract (an adjacent route, configuration or caller) and state that boundary in the claim. Measured only inside its contract, closed is true by definition while the next round finds the neighbour.
ops.why: LC-1: my final goal-check called both classes closed as a class with no probe beyond the contract, and adjacent members surfaced from readers who probed outside it; distinct from P-06, which re-measures a failed premise but never tests the boundary.
Displaced by G-22: narrowest Gotcha (git status on ignored paths), rarely reached from a pm seat.

ops.entry: WHEN a criterion promises every invocation converges, recovers or checks something DO trace each entry path to where that mechanism runs: a preflight that refuses before reaching the shared core skips it, so a re-run never converges. Grade per entry path, not by the core alone.
ops.why: Observation: two verbs refused in lock-free preflight before the core, so recovery placed only in the core would never have run on re-run; general to any per-invocation guarantee.

originals.original: WHEN goal-checking a production fix outside the signed task file lists DO report a scope finding even if a divergence ledger calls it fixed in passing; evidence can explain a change, but cannot grant task ownership or operator approval.

WHEN a criterion detects change by git status DO run git check-ignore on the paths first: git reports an ignored path as untracked and never as modified, so the clause returns the same answer whether the corpus was rewritten or not. Hash a recorded manifest instead.
